newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan body says problem loan purchases falling.
newsitem.headline: Japan body says problem loan purchases falling.

text.p: Japan's Cooperative Credit Purchasing Co Ltd (CCPC), a body set up by more than 160 domestic financial institutions to buy problem loans and recover those loans, said on Monday that its purchases of problem loans had peaked and were now falling.

"The number and value of problem loans that we bought in the first half (of 1996/97) fell sharply from the second half of 1995/96. So we think our purchases have peaked out both in number and in value," CCPC president Akira Kanazawa said.
In the first half of 1996/97 ended September 30, CCPC bought 724 problem loans for 224.3 billion yen against their combined book value of 782.5 billion yen, the body said.
In the second half of 1995/96, it bought 1,823 property-backed problem loans with a combined book value of 2.24 trillion yen.
Set up by Japanese financial institutions in January 1993, the CCPC's aim is to help financial institutions smoothly dispose of their property-backed problem loans.
The CCPC buys problem loans and the backing collateral from financial institutions at a discount based on the market value.
The institutions selling loans to the CCPC post tax-exempt losses equal to the difference between the book value and the purchase price.
Since March 1993, the CCPC has bought 9,075 problem loans for 5.23 trillion yen against a total book value of 12.92 trillion yen.
However, property market analysts say recovering problem loans through sales of the collateralised real estate remain slow because of the protracted slump in Japan's real estate market.
In the first half of 1996/97, the CCPC recovered 171 billion yen worth of problem loans, of which 158.8 billion yen came through sales of 1,040 lots of collateralised real estate, the CCPC said.
Since it started operations, the CCPC has recovered 602.6 billion yen worth of problem loans, of which 557.2 billion yen came through sales of 3,055 lots of collateralised real estate, it said.
"Our body has a limited term, focusing on problem loan purchases for the first five years and then focusing on recovering property-backed problem loans," said Kanazawa.
"However, as the purchases have peaked out, we will concentrate on recovering (such problem loans)."
